title: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) for fluid mechanics: A review
authors_full: Shengze Cai, Zhiping Mao, Zhicheng Wang, Minglang Yin, George Em Karniadakis
affiliations: Division of Applied Mathematics, Brown University, Providence, RI 02912, USA (Cai, Karniadakis); School of Mathematical Sciences, Xiamen University, 361005 China (Mao); Laboratory of Ocean Energy Utilization of Ministry of Education, Dalian University of Technology, Dalian, 116024, China (Wang); School of Engineering, Brown University, Providence, RI 02912, USA (Yin, Karniadakis); Center for Biomedical Engineering, Brown University, Providence, RI 02912, USA (Yin, Karniadakis)
verification: verified in inventory; arXiv preprint PDF (arXiv:2105.09506v1 [physics.flu-dyn], 20 May 2021) read in full (12 pages)
subdomain: inverse problems in fluid mechanics: 3D wake past circular cylinder (Re=200) reconstructed from 2D2C planar observations, 2D supersonic bow shock (M_infinity=4) from density gradients, thrombus permeability inference (Navier-Stokes + Cahn-Hilliard); reviews incompressible, compressible, biomedical and turbulent flow PINNs
industry_context: CFD software ecosystem (OpenFOAM cited as >100,000 lines of code; NVIDIA SimNet library cited as efficient PINN implementation); flow-diagnostics industries (planar PIV, Schlieren photography, pressure sensors as data sources); biomedical thrombosis modeling; academic (Brown University group)
physics_enforced_exact: Dimensional incompressible Navier-Stokes (momentum + continuity) at Re=200: f_{1,2,3} = du/dt + (u.grad)u + grad(p) - (1/Re)laplacian(u), f_4 = div(u) (Eqs. 5-6); 2D compressible Euler: div(f(U)) = 0, U = [rho, rho*u, rho*v, rho*E]^T with G1 = [rho*u, p+rho*u^2, rho*u*v, u(rho*E+p)]^T, G2 = [rho*v, rho*u*v, p+rho*v^2, v(rho*E+p)]^T, closed by polytropic equation of state p = (gamma-1)(rho*E - (1/2)rho|u|^2) (Eqs. 8-9); thrombus: Navier-Stokes with viscous stress sigma_vis = mu*grad(u) and cohesive stress sigma_coh = lambda*div(grad(phi) (x) phi) coupled to Cahn-Hilliard phase-field: rho(du/dt + u.grad u) + grad p = div(sigma_vis + sigma_coh) - mu(1-phi)u/(2*kappa(phi)), div(u)=0, dpsi/dt + u.grad psi = 0, dphi/dt + u.grad phi = tau*Delta(omega), omega = Delta(phi) + gamma*g(phi) (Eqs. 12-16)
pde_type: multiple (incompressible NS (parabolic/elliptic mixed), compressible Euler (hyperbolic), Cahn-Hilliard phase-field (parabolic, 4th-order))
dimensionality: 3D+time (wake: space-time input (x,y,z,t) over sub-domain [1.5,7.5]x[-3,3]x[4,9]); 2D steady (bow shock); 2D+time (thrombus)
nonlinearity: strongly nonlinear (convective term (u.grad)u of NS, nonlinear fluxes of compressible Euler, phase-field double-well coupling and permeability law kappa(phi)=exp(a*phi)+b)
bcs_ic_handled: 3D wake (inverse): boundary and initial conditions NOT required - only data loss on a few observed cross-planes (Table 1: x-plane (v,w) 61x26, y-plane (u,w) 61x26, z-plane (u,v) 61x61; no pressure data). Bow shock: instead of most classical CFD boundary conditions (unknown in high-speed experiments), uses inflow conditions (M_inf=4, p_inf=101253.6 Pa, rho_inf=1.225 kg/m^3, u_inf=1360.6963 m/s, v_inf=0, T_inf=288K), velocity condition on body surface, limited surface-pressure sensor data, density gradients in sub-domain D (Schlieren-motivated), plus global mass, momentum and energy constraints. Thrombus: Dirichlet parabolic inlet u=g1(x,t) on Gamma1 x (0,T), no-slip on walls, Neumann BCs dphi/dn = domega/dn = 0 at all boundaries, plus initial-snapshot data
enforcement_mechanism: soft-penalty - physics enters as MSE residual terms in a weighted loss; Remark 1: loss definition is problem-dependent and PINNs can solve over-determined systems (initial/boundary conditions known plus interior/boundary measurements); inverse problems require the data loss for well-posedness
enforcement_details: MLP u~(x,t) differentiated via automatic differentiation (AD) to compute exact partial derivatives (no truncation error vs numerical approximations) and form residuals f(x,t;u,du,d2u,...;lambda) of the governing operators; unknown PDE parameters lambda (e.g., permeability kappa for thrombus) trained simultaneously with network parameters theta by minimizing the total loss; bow-shock case replaces classical BCs by a density-gradient loss (restricted to sub-domain D, unlike the whole-domain gradients of ref [13]), global integral constraints (mass, momentum, energy) and surface pressure; thrombus uses two coupled fully-connected networks (Net U: outputs u,v,p,phi; Net W: outputs psi,omega1,omega2) and learns kappa(phi)=exp(a*phi)+b with a,b optimized
network_architecture: 3D wake: fully-connected MLP, 8 hidden layers x 200 neurons per layer, input (x,y,z,t) -> outputs (u,v,w,p). Bow shock: 6x60 MLP (6 hidden layers, 60 neurons) with layer-wise adaptive tanh activation. Thrombus: two fully-connected networks Net U (u,v,p,phi) and Net W (psi,omega1,omega2), each 4 hidden layers x 20 neurons. Review also surveys hp-VPINN (variational/Galerkin), cPINN, XPINN, hard-constraint networks, CNN-based PINNs, multi-fidelity composite networks, Bayesian PINNs, and NVIDIA SimNet
activation_function: sin(.) for the 3D wake case; layer-wise adaptive tanh for the bow-shock case; thrombus activation not stated
input_representation: space-time coordinates (x,y,z,t) for the 3D wake; (x,t) for the thrombus; bow-shock network inputs not explicitly stated (steady problem); no extra features beyond coordinates
output_representation: wake: velocity and pressure (u,v,w,p) - pressure inferred with zero pressure data; bow shock: density, pressure and velocity fields inferred from density gradients; thrombus: Net U outputs u,v,p,phi and Net W outputs auxiliary field psi and omega1,omega2; permeability parameterized as kappa(phi)=exp(a*phi)+b with a,b learned (Eq. 24)
loss_terms: General (Eq. 3): L = omega1*L_PDE + omega2*L_data + omega3*L_IC + omega4*L_BC, each an MSE/L2-norm over sampled points. Wake (Eqs. 4-6): L = L_data + L_PDE; L_data = (1/Nu)sum||u~ - u_data||^2 + (1/Nv)sum||v~ - v_data||^2 + (1/Nw)sum||w~ - w_data||^2 on observed planes; L_PDE = (1/Nf)sum_i sum_j ||f_j(x_i^r, t_i^r)||^2 with f_{1,2,3} = du/dt + (u.grad)u + grad(p) - (1/Re)laplacian(u) and f_4 = div(u). Bow shock (Eq. 10): Loss = omega1*Loss_f + omega2*Loss_grad_rho + omega3*Loss_inflow + omega4*Loss_p_s + omega5*(Loss_Mass + Loss_Momentum + Loss_Energy) + omega6*Loss_w. Thrombus (Eqs. 19-23): L = omega1*L_PDE + omega2*L_IC + omega3*L_BC + omega4*L_data, with B combining Dirichlet and Neumann residuals
loss_weighting: wake: fixed, all weighting coefficients equal to 1; bow shock: dynamic weights technique (refs [36,11], Wang et al. gradient-pathology work); thrombus: weights omega1-omega4 values not specified (PDE loss dominant during training)
sampling_strategy: wake: N_f = 3x10^6 residual points randomly sampled over sub-domain Omega_c = [1.5,7.5] x [-3,3] x [4,9]; data from observed cross-planes (50 snapshots with dt=0.2, about two vortex-shedding periods). Thrombus: 1,000 points from an initial snapshot, 10,000 inner points for PDE residuals, 1,000 boundary points; point measurements and inner points drawn from the spatio-temporal domain; training data from 30 snapshots t in [0.03, 0.93]
optimizer_schedule: ADAM (adaptive gradient-based first-order, Kingma & Ba) throughout. Wake: mini-batch size N=10^4 for both data and residual points; 150 epochs with learning rates 1e-3, 5e-4, 1e-4 every 50 epochs. Bow shock: Adam, learning rate 6e-4, 3x10^5 epochs. Thrombus: 300,000 epochs
domain_decomposition: none in the authors' own case studies; review discusses variational hp-VPINN with domain decomposition [24], cPINN [25], XPINN [26], a parallel domain-decomposition PINN implementation for flow problems [27], and NVIDIA SimNet [28]; summary calls for efficient multi-GPU (data + model parallel) implementations for industrial-scale problems
transfer_or_pretraining: none used in the case studies; summary proposes transfer learning to predict fast flow at a new high Reynolds number given available solutions at lower Reynolds numbers, and closure models for unresolved high-Re dynamics via the PINN data-assimilation method
uq_method: none in the authors' own cases; review notes uncertainty quantification of PDE solutions inferred by neural networks studied via a Bayesian framework (refs [29-33], incl. B-PINN [33])
data_regime: physics + simulation data, sparse planar observations: 3D wake - 2D2C velocity observations on 3-5 cross-planes (61x26 / 61x61 grids) from Nektar spectral/hp CFD snapshots (reference simulation until time=10); bow shock - steady CFD density gradients in sub-domain D, limited surface-pressure points, inflow conditions; thrombus - synthetic CFD phase-field + point-measurement data from 30 snapshots; no experimental data in the authors' own cases (experimental Schlieren/PIV only motivate the data types mimicked)
datasets_used: own cases: 3D wake over circular cylinder at Re=200 (Nektar spectral/hp element CFD reference); 2D bow shock at M_inf=4 (CFD reference); 2D semi-circular thrombus in channel with steady parabolic inflow (CFD reference; thrombus model adapted from refs [55-58]); reviewed literature cases include NSFnet [11], Hidden Fluid Mechanics / Schlieren flow visualization [12], compressible high-speed flows [13], thrombus material inference [14], 4D-flow-MRI cardiovascular PINN [42], heat transfer PINN [45], tomographic espresso-cup 3D flow [46], free-boundary/Stefan problems [47], turbulent natural convection [48], mRFS multiphysics [49], sparse-data blood flow [50]
baselines_compared: CFD references: Nektar spectral/hp element method solver (3D wake), CFD solver for the bow shock (inlet condition 11) and the thrombus; PINN fields compared point-wise against CFD fields; narrative comparison PINNs vs traditional CFD (FEM/FVM/spectral/meshless, OpenFOAM): PINNs superior at integrating scattered data and ill-posed/inverse problems, inferior for standard forward problems
evaluation_metrics: relative L2-norm error e_V = ||V_CFD - V~||^2 / ||V_CFD||^2 x 100% (Eq. 7) computed over the entire investigated domain and time; qualitative comparison of vorticity iso-surfaces (|omega| = 1.2) and point time-series; inferred parameter values (a, b, kappa) vs ground truth; loss histories per term
key_quantitative_results: 3D wake (Re=200): with 5 or 4 observed cross-planes (Cases 1-2) PINNs infer full 3D u,v,w,p accurately - streamwise-velocity relative L2 error mostly <25%; with only 3 planes (Case 3) errors become much larger but main flow features still recovered; inferred vorticity |omega|=1.2 iso-surfaces at t=8.0 consistent with CFD. Bow shock (M_inf=4): PINN pressure and u fields in good agreement with CFD using only density gradients + surface pressure + inflow + global mass/momentum/energy constraints. Thrombus: inferred permeability law kappa(phi)=exp(a*phi)+b with a=7.10, b=0.0003 (true: 6.90, 0.0); kappa(phi=-1)=0.0011 vs reference 0.001 and kappa(phi=0)=1.0003 vs reference 1; all loss components except the PDE loss below O(10^-3) after 300,000 epochs
errors_reported: 3D wake: relative L2 of streamwise velocity mostly <25% (Cases 1-2); Case 3 errors much larger (shown as curves in Fig. 4, not tabulated); w-velocity errors larger than the other components (small magnitude); larger errors at initial and final instants (no training data for derivatives at t<0 and t>10). Thrombus: inferred a=7.10 vs true 6.90; b=0.0003 vs true 0.0; kappa(phi=-1)=0.0011 vs 0.001; kappa(phi=0)=1.0003 vs 1; losses other than PDE loss lower than O(10^-3)
speedup_claims: none quantified; explicit statement that the current generation of PINNs is NOT as accurate or efficient as high-order CFD codes for standard forward problems; cites very good parallel speed-up of domain-decomposed PINN flow simulations [27] and suggests PINNs may in future tackle industrial-complexity problems at scale that CFD methods cannot
ablations: observational-budget ablation in the 3D wake: number/placement of observed 2D2C planes varied (Case 1: 5 planes, Case 2: 4 planes, Case 3: 3 planes) - accuracy degrades as planes decrease (Case 1 slightly better than Case 2; Case 3 much worse); bow-shock setup ablates data sources vs prior work [13] by restricting density-gradient data to sub-domain D instead of the whole computational domain
stated_limitations: p.1: 'PINNs are not meant to be a replacement of existing CFD codes, and in fact the current generation of PINNs is not as accurate or as efficient as high-order CFD codes for solving the standard forward problems' - attributed to minimization of a high-dimensional non-convex loss, 'a grand challenge of all neural networks even commercial machine learning'. Summary (Sec. 6): existing CFD solvers cannot handle the ill-posed scenario where data exist but BCs/ICs are unknown, so PINNs are 'a complementary approach' for idealized problems. Wake reconstruction degrades with fewer observation planes and at time instants lacking derivative data (no IC provided). kappa(phi) relation acknowledged as non-unique in form (only values at phi=0 and phi=-1 matter). Open challenges listed: active flow control, replacing expensive experiments, transfer learning across Re, closure models at very high Re, multi-GPU scaling
failure_modes: training difficulty from high-dimensional non-convex loss minimization (authors' stated general NN limitation); error blow-up in 3D wake Case 3 (only 3 observation planes); poorly reconstructed w-velocity due to small magnitude; larger discrepancy at initial/final times when the IC is not provided in the unsteady case (also noted via ref [12]); review cites gradient pathologies [36] and the NTK analysis 'When and why PINNs fail to train' [41] as known training/convergence issues
reproducibility: no code or data URL given in the PDF; arXiv preprint 2105.09506; full hyperparameters per case stated (layers, neurons, activation, epochs, learning rates, batch size, sampling counts, all loss-term definitions); reference data generated with the open spectral/hp solver Nektar; NVIDIA SimNet [28] mentioned as an efficient PINN implementation library
quotable_finding: The main attractive advantage of PINNs in solving fluid mechanics problems is that a unified framework (shown in Fig. 1) can be used for both forward and inverse problems. (p. 4)
relevance_rqs: RQ1: fluids/aerospace + biomedical inverse flow problems (wake reconstruction from planar PIV-like data, supersonic flow from Schlieren-like gradients, thrombosis); RQ2: canonical component survey - MLP backbone, sin/adaptive-tanh activations, multi-term MSE losses, dynamic weights, ADAM schedules, cPINN/XPINN decomposition, Bayesian UQ; RQ3: exact NS/Euler/Cahn-Hilliard residual enforcement via AD soft penalties, replacing classical BCs with data + global integral constraints; RQ4: a domain review itself - positioning vs CFD, honest limitations, failure modes, and future-challenge agenda
manuscript_section: S5 domain applications (fluids inverse problems); S4 methods overview (canonical PINN formulation, Fig. 1 and Eq. 3); review-landscape synthesis tables (T1 domain table; T3 reliability/limitations); F2 loss-design discussion
cross_paper_links: builds-on: PINN-A01 (Raissi, Perdikaris, Karniadakis JCP 2019, cited as ref [15]; original PINN part I/II as refs [19,20]); cites PINN-B07 (XPINN, Jagtap & Karniadakis, ref [26]); cites PINN-A06 (Wang, Yu, Perdikaris, 'When and why PINNs fail to train: A neural tangent kernel perspective', ref [41]); compares-to/reviews: NSFnet [11] (Cai et al.), Hidden Fluid Mechanics [12], compressible-flow PINN [13] (Mao, Jagtap, Karniadakis), thrombus PINN [14] (Yin et al.), cPINN [25], hp-VPINN [24], B-PINN [33], adaptive activation functions [35], gradient pathologies / dynamic weights [36], multifidelity composite networks [34], NVIDIA SimNet [28], RL bluff-body flow control [59]
notes_caveats: All three new case studies are inverse problems on synthetic CFD data only - no experimental validation in the authors' own cases (Schlieren/PIV merely motivate the data types); the review is narrative without systematic search methodology; wake errors are shown as curves (Fig. 4), not tabulated, so exact error values are unavailable and 'mostly less than 25%' is a qualitative claim; thrombus loss weights unspecified - weakens reproducibility; inverse permeability parameterization non-unique (authors acknowledge); despite the 'review' title, substantial new results (3 case studies) are included; strong companion piece to HFM (PINN-C01) from the same group
